title: Field tests: time trials, all-out efforts and running tests
goal: Choose and run a field test (time trial, 3-min all-out test, critical-power efforts, Cooper or Yo-Yo), and control the power meter and the weather so the result means something.

steps.title: Time trials in the field

claims.text: In 8 trained male cyclists, 4-min and 20-min time trials were reliable (20-min typical error 4.6 W, ICC 0.99), and 20-min power was strongly associated with 60-min power (R² 0.92).

evidence.quote: The 4-min MPO (R2 = .95), 20-min MPO (R2 = .92), estimated CP (R2 = .82), and combination of the 4- and 20-min MPO (adjusted R2 = .98) were strongly associated with the 60-min MPO

steps.title: The 3-minute all-out test
steps.text:
The [3-min all-out test](g:three-minute-all-out-test) (3MT) needs no pacing: go flat out from the start and keep going. Power falls, then levels off. The mean power over the last 30 s is the [end-test power](g:end-test-power) (EP), and the work done above it estimates [W′](g:w-prime).

In the original study of 10 active people, EP (287 W) matched [critical power](g:critical-power) (287 W) from five rides to exhaustion [[c:3mt-original]]. A 2026 [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 20 studies found EP repeatable, but on average **higher** than CP, more so in highly trained athletes, while the W′ estimate ran low [[c:3mt-meta]].

To get a usable result: a full practice trial first, strong encouragement, and no clock in view [[c:3mt-rules]].

claims.text: In 10 habitually active adults, 3-min all-out end-test power (287 ± 55 W) did not differ from critical power (287 ± 56 W), agreeing within 5 W in 8 of 10.

evidence.quote: The EP was 287 +/- 55 W, which was not significantly different from, and highly correlated with, CP (287 +/- 56 W; P = 0.37, r = 0.99).
in 8 of 10 cases, EP agreed with CP to within 5 W.

claims.text: Across 20 small studies, end-test power was reliable (ICC 0.89–0.99) but systematically overestimated CP, especially in highly trained athletes, while work above EP underestimated W′.

evidence.quote: Test-retest reliability demonstrated 'good' to 'excellent' agreement for EP (ICC = 0.89-0.99) and WEP (ICC = 0.76-0.98). EP systematically overestimates CP
Especially in PL4/5 athletes, EP seems to largely overestimate CP.

claims.text: A full familiarisation trial and strong verbal encouragement are needed for a usable 3-min all-out test, with no time-based feedback.

evidence.quote: Familiarisation trials and proper verbal encouragement during the 3-min test are mandatory.
additional aspects, such as high motivational state, appropriate cadence throughout the test, and the absence of any time-based feedback should be considered.

debate.question: Can the 3-min all-out test stand in for critical power?

sides.position: Roughly, yes: in its first test EP matched CP within about 5 W in 8 of 10 people, from a single visit.
Not reliably: EP overestimates CP by an amount that depends on the protocol and the athlete, so use EP as a marker in its own right.

steps.title: Critical power from a few field efforts
steps.text:
Critical power can also come from several maximal efforts of different lengths, fitted with the models of the next module. The choices matter: the duration and number of efforts, the rest between them and the model all change the CP you get [[c:cp-choices]].

In the field, cyclists did maximal efforts of 3, 7 and 12 min: in one session with 30 min rest between, or on separate days, or taken as their best 3, 7 and 12 min from training and racing. Against lab CP the error was about 4.5–6%, and repeat tests varied by 2.4–6.5% [[c:field-cp]].

So field CP is usable, but the protocol is part of the number: keep it the same each time.

claims.text: The duration, number and recovery of the efforts, and the model used, all affect the CP and W′ obtained.

evidence.quote: However, the duration, number, and recovery between predictive CWR and the mathematical model (hyperbolic or derived linear models) are known to affect CP and W'.

claims.text: Field CP from 3-, 7- and 12-min maximal efforts (same day, separate days or from training data) had a standard error against lab CP of 4.5–5.8% and a test–retest CV of 2.4–6.5%.

evidence.quote: Standard error of the estimate of CP was 4.5, 5.8 and 5.2 % for experiments 1-3, respectively.
Mean coefficient of variation in field CP was 2.4, 6.5 and 3.5 % for experiments 1-3, respectively.

steps.title: Running tests: Cooper and Yo-Yo
steps.text:
Running has two classic field tests.

The [Cooper test](g:cooper-test) estimates [VO2max](g:vo2max) from the distance run in 12 min. In a meta-analysis of 123 studies, the 12-min run [correlated](g:correlation) r = 0.78 with measured VO2max, among the best of the walk and run tests. It gives an estimate, not a measurement [[c:cooper]].

The [Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test](g:yo-yo-test) measures repeated hard running with short rests. It tracks changes in performance better than VO2max does, but it was built for intermittent sports such as football [[c:yoyo]]. For a road runner, a TT is closer to the race.

How good is r = 0.78? Square it: r² is the share of the differences between people that the test accounts for.

claims.text: Walk/run field tests estimate VO2max with low to moderate validity (r 0.42–0.79); the 12-min run (r 0.78) and 1.5-mile run (r 0.79) were best, and the score is only an estimate.

evidence.quote: The overall results showed that the criterion-related validity of the walk/run tests for estimating maximum oxygen uptake ranged from low to moderate (rp = 0.42-0.79), with the 1.5 mile (rp = 0.79, 0.73-0.85) and 12 min walk/run tests (rp = 0.78, 0.72-0.83) having the higher criterion-related validity for distance- and time-based field tests, respectively.
evaluators must be aware that the performance score of the walk/run field tests is simply an estimation and not a direct measure of cardiorespiratory fitness.

claims.text: The Yo-Yo intermittent recovery tests assess repeated intense exercise in intermittent sports and are more sensitive to changes in performance than VO2max.

evidence.quote: The two Yo-Yo intermittent recovery (IR) tests evaluate an individual's ability to repeatedly perform intense exercise.
The Yo-Yo IR tests have shown to be a more sensitive measure of changes in performance than maximum oxygen uptake.

steps.title: What does r = 0.78 explain?
steps.problem: The 12-min run correlates r = 0.78 with lab VO2max. What share of the differences in VO2max between people does it account for?
steps: The run accounts for about 61% of the differences in VO2max between people; the other 39% comes from things it doesn't capture, such as [running economy](g:running-economy), pacing, motivation and measurement error.
Good enough to rank a group; rough for predicting one runner's VO2max.

steps.title: Power meters and the weather
steps.text:
**Power meters.** Against a reference, 54 meters were off by −0.9 ± 3.2% on average, and 6 by more than 5%; repeat readings varied by only about 1.2% [[c:pm-trueness]]. So a meter can track you well and still disagree with your friend's, or your next one.

**[Zero offset](g:zero-offset).** Temperature shifted readings by 5.2% (SRM) and 8.4% (PowerTap) [[c:pm-temp]]. Zero the meter with the cranks unloaded, after it has had time to reach the outside temperature, just before the test.

**Weather.** In a 15-min time trial at 40 °C, cyclists did about 17% less work than at 21 °C [[c:heat-tt]]. Wind, rain and gradient matter too: same course, similar weather, or test indoors.

claims.text: 54 power meters deviated from a first-principles reference by −0.9 ± 3.2% (6 by more than ±5%), with high precision (CV 1.2 ± 0.9%); some brands read about 5% lower than an SRM in some conditions.

evidence.quote: The mean deviations of the power meters were -0.9±3.2% (mean±SD) with 6 power meters deviating by more than±5%. The coefficients of variation of the power meters were 1.2±0.9% (mean±SD)
The STG PO was significantly lower than the SRM PO in the heavy-exercise-intensity zone (zone 2, -5.1%) and the low part of the severe-intensity zone (zone 3, -4.9%).

claims.text: Power meter readings were noticeably affected by temperature (5.2% for SRM, 8.4% for PowerTap); calibration matching test conditions, including temperature, is advised.

evidence.quote: power output readings were noticeably influenced by temperature (5.2% for SRM and 8.4% for PT).
Calibration procedures matching performance tests (duration, power, cadence, and temperature) are, however, advised as the error associated with each unit may vary.

claims.text: In 8 men, total work in a 15-min cycling time trial was about 17% lower at 40 °C than at 21 °C.

evidence.quote: Total work performed in HOT (147.7 +/- 23.9 kJ) was approximately 17% less
total work is significantly reduced by heat stress because of a gradual slowing of pace over time.

points: Field time trials (4 or 20 min on the bike, 3 or 5 km running) are repeatable and close to racing if course, warm-up, pacing and timing stay the same.
The 3-min all-out test gives end-test power and an estimate of W′ in one visit; EP is repeatable but tends to sit above CP, especially in trained athletes.
Field CP from 3-, 7- and 12-min maximal efforts is usable (CV 2.4–6.5%); the protocol is part of the number.
The Cooper test only estimates VO2max (r = 0.78, so r² ≈ 0.61); the Yo-Yo test suits intermittent sports more than road running.
Power meters can be precise yet several % off: zero them at outside temperature and retest on the same meter, on the same course, in similar weather.

variants.stem: A runner wants to track her aerobic fitness every 6 weeks in the field, with as little noise as possible. Which test should she use?

options.text: A 5 km time trial on the same track, after a practice run
options.why: Right: a time trial on a fixed course is repeatable and close to racing, and the practice run removes the learning effect.

options.text: Running to exhaustion at her goal 10 km pace
options.why: Time-to-exhaustion tests vary by more than 10% from try to try: far too noisy.

options.text: A parkrun on a different course each time
options.why: Changing the course changes hills, surface and turns, so times can't be compared.

options.text: Her heart rate during an easy jog
options.why: Easy-run heart rate swings with sleep, heat and hydration and says little about race fitness.

variants.stem: In a 3-min all-out test, what is the power over the last 30 s meant to estimate?

options.text: Critical power
options.why: Right: once W′ is spent, the power you can still hold is close to CP.

options.text: W′
options.why: W′ is the work done above end-test power, an amount in kJ, not a power.

options.text: Peak sprint power
options.why: Peak power comes in the first seconds of the test, not the last 30 s.

options.text: VO2max
options.why: The 3MT is a power test; VO2max needs gas measurements.

variants.stem: The 2007 study that proposed end-test power = critical power tested 10 habitually active people. A coach wants to use EP as CP for national-level cyclists. What most limits that?

options.text: A small, less-trained sample; later data show EP overshoots CP in trained riders
options.why: Right: 10 active people can't show how the test behaves in elite riders, and the 2026 meta-analysis found EP above CP, most in highly trained athletes.

options.text: Nothing: r = 0.99 proves EP equals CP for anyone
options.why: A high correlation shows the two rise together, not that they are equal in every person or group.

options.text: It had no placebo group, so its results are invalid
options.why: A placebo isn't needed to compare two measures in the same people; the problem is who was tested.

options.text: It was published too long ago to be trusted
options.why: Age alone doesn't make a study wrong; what matters is its sample and whether later work agrees.

variants.stem: A rider holds back in the first minute of her 3-min all-out test and finishes with a strong last 30 s. What happens to her end-test power?

options.text: It comes out too high, above her CP
options.why: Right: W′ wasn't spent early, so the last 30 s still include work above CP.

options.text: It comes out too low, below her CP
options.why: Pacing saves W′ for the end, which raises the final power, not lowers it.

options.text: It is unchanged: EP doesn't depend on pacing
options.why: The test only works if W′ is used up before the last 30 s; pacing breaks that.

options.text: It becomes a better estimate of W′
options.why: EP is a power; and holding back makes the work-above-EP estimate of W′ worse, not better.

variants.stem: A triathlete wants a field CP for her bike without a lab. Which plan follows a protocol that was tested against lab CP?

options.text: Maximal 3-, 7- and 12-min efforts, 30 min rest between
options.why: Right: this field protocol gave CP within about 5% of lab values and repeated within 2.4%.

options.text: One 20-min all-out effort, then take 95% of it
options.why: That is the FTP protocol; FTP and CP are different numbers.

options.text: Maximal 30-s, 1-min and 2-min efforts
options.why: No field protocol tested against lab CP used efforts this short; they lean mostly on W′, which skews the fitted CP.

options.text: One evenly paced 3-min effort
options.why: One effort gives one point on the curve; a paced 3 min isn't the all-out 3MT either.

variants.stem: The 1.5-mile run correlates r = 0.79 with lab VO2max. What share of the differences in VO2max between people does it account for?

options.text: About 62%
About 79%
options.why: This uses r itself; the share accounted for is r², which is smaller.

options.text: About 89%
options.why: This takes the square root of r (√0.79 = 0.89) instead of squaring it.

options.text: About 21%
options.why: This takes 1 − r; that isn't the share accounted for (and 1 − r² would be the unexplained share, 38%).

variants.stem: The weakest walk/run test in the meta-analysis correlated r = 0.42 with lab VO2max. What share of the differences in VO2max between people does it account for?

options.text: About 18%
About 42%
options.why: This uses r itself; the share accounted for is r², which is smaller.

options.text: About 65%
options.why: This takes the square root of r (√0.42 = 0.65) instead of squaring it.

options.text: About 58%
options.why: This takes 1 − r; that isn't the share accounted for (1 − r² = 82% would be the unexplained share).

variants.stem: A marathon runner's club offers a monthly Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test. Is it the best way to track her marathon fitness?

options.text: No: it targets intermittent sports; a time trial fits her event better
options.why: Right: the Yo-Yo measures repeated hard running with short rests, the demand of football, not of a steady marathon.

options.text: Yes: it is more sensitive than VO2max, so it beats any test
options.why: More sensitive than VO2max isn't the same as best for her event; a steady time trial matches the marathon's demand.

options.text: Yes: any running test tracks any running event equally
options.why: Tests track what they demand: short, repeated sprints aren't marathon running.

options.text: No: field tests can't track fitness; only lab tests can
options.why: Field time trials are repeatable and valid; the issue is which field test fits the event.

variants.stem: A rider keeps his bike in a 20 °C flat, rides out into 4 °C air, zeroes the power meter at the door and starts a 20-min test 5 min later. What's the problem?

options.text: He zeroed it before it cooled to the outside temperature
options.why: Right: temperature shifts readings, so zero after the meter has settled to outside air, just before the test.

options.text: None: zeroing indoors is the most accurate
options.why: Indoor zeroing sets the meter for 20 °C; at 4 °C its readings drift.

options.text: He should zero it while pedalling hard
options.why: Zeroing needs the cranks unloaded: it sets the reading for zero force.

options.text: Cold makes power meters read exactly zero
options.why: Cold shifts readings by several %, it doesn't zero them.

variants.stem: A cyclist's 20-min power was 300 W on her old crank meter and 315 W on a new pedal meter a month later. Is the 5% gain real?

options.text: Can't tell: meters can disagree by more than 5%
options.why: Right: meters were off by −0.9 ± 3.2% on average and some by over 5%, so a meter change alone can explain 15 W.

options.text: Yes: both meters repeat to about 1%
options.why: Repeating well (precision) isn't agreeing with each other (trueness); each can be steady and still differ.

options.text: Yes: newer meters are always more accurate
options.why: Newness doesn't guarantee accuracy; meters of all ages vary in trueness.

options.text: No: pedal meters always read high
options.why: There's no fixed rule by meter type; you only know by testing both against a reference.

variants.stem: A triathlete's FTP is 250 W on her road bike's meter and 262 W on her time-trial bike's meter, tested a week apart. Best reading of the gap?

options.text: Mostly the meters: they can differ by about 5%
options.why: Right: 12 W is about 5%, within the spread between meters; test both bikes on one meter to know.

options.text: She is 5% fitter on the time-trial bike
options.why: This assumes the two meters agree, which they often don't.

options.text: She gained 12 W of fitness in a week
options.why: A week is too short for a 5% gain, and the meters changed too.

options.text: The road bike meter must be broken
options.why: A 5% gap is ordinary between working meters; neither needs to be faulty.

variants.stem: A runner's 5 km time trial on the same track took 19:00 in April at 12 °C and 19:40 in July at 31 °C. Best interpretation?

options.text: The heat can explain the slower time
options.why: Right: heat cut work by about 17% in a 15-min time trial; compare tests run in similar conditions.

options.text: She has lost fitness since April
options.why: Possible, but the 19 °C hotter day can explain a 3.5% slower time by itself.

options.text: Heat only matters in races over an hour
options.why: Performance fell in a 15-min time trial in the heat, without large rises in core temperature.

options.text: Warm muscles are faster, so she lost even more
options.why: A good warm-up helps, but hot weather slows endurance efforts; it doesn't speed them up.
